guide.summary: Unit 8 (c. 1914–present, focused on 1914–1945) covers the causes, conduct, and consequences of World War I; the Russian Revolution; the peace settlement; interwar instability, the Great Depression, and the rise of fascism, Nazism, and Stalinism; the road to and conduct of World War II; the Holocaust; and 20th-century cultural and intellectual developments.

sections.heading: World War I
sections.body: Long-term causes included militarism, alliance systems (Triple Alliance and Triple Entente), imperial rivalry, and nationalism, especially in the Balkans; the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (June 1914) triggered a chain of mobilizations and declarations of war. On the Western Front, trench warfare and new technologies (machine guns, artillery, poison gas, tanks, airplanes) produced stalemate and massive casualties (Verdun, the Somme). Total war mobilized entire economies and societies: governments controlled production, rationed goods, used propaganda, and drew women into new kinds of work. The war became global through empires and the entry of the Ottoman Empire and, in 1917, the United States.

sections.heading: Russian Revolution
sections.body: Wartime defeats, food shortages, and the tsar's discredited leadership led to the February Revolution (1917), which ended the monarchy and created a Provisional Government that continued the war. Lenin's Bolsheviks, promising 'peace, land, and bread,' seized power in the October Revolution, withdrew from the war through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (1918), and won the Russian Civil War. War Communism gave way to the New Economic Policy (1921), which allowed limited private trade. Stalin later imposed Five-Year Plans for rapid industrialization and forced collectivization of agriculture, causing famine (including in Ukraine), and used purges, show trials, and the Gulag in the Great Terror.

sections.heading: Peace settlement and interwar crises
sections.body: The Paris Peace Conference produced the Treaty of Versailles (1919): Germany accepted responsibility for the war (Article 231), paid reparations, lost territory and colonies, and was disarmed; the League of Nations was created, but the United States didn't join. The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires were dismantled; new states emerged in Eastern Europe under the principle of self-determination, and mandates placed former Ottoman lands under British and French control. Resentment, economic dislocation, hyperinflation in Germany (1923), and the Great Depression (from 1929) undermined democracies. Mussolini's Fascists took power in Italy (1922) with a one-party state glorifying the nation. Hitler became German chancellor in 1933 and built a totalitarian state based on racial antisemitism, terror, and propaganda (Nuremberg Laws, 1935). The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) became a testing ground for fascist and Soviet intervention.

sections.heading: World War II and the Holocaust
sections.body: Hitler remilitarized the Rhineland (1936) and annexed Austria (1938); Britain and France pursued appeasement at Munich (1938), allowing Germany to take the Sudetenland. The Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939) preceded the invasion of Poland, which began the war. Germany's blitzkrieg conquered much of Europe; the Battle of Britain halted invasion plans; Germany invaded the USSR (1941), and the Soviets' victory at Stalingrad (1942–1943) turned the tide. The Allies landed in Normandy (June 1944), and Germany surrendered in May 1945. The Holocaust, the Nazi genocide of about six million Jews along with Roma, disabled people, and others, escalated from persecution to mass shootings and death camps. Intellectual and cultural life reflected crisis: Freud's psychology, Einstein's relativity, modernist art, and literature of disillusionment.

keyTakeaways: WWI causes: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism + Sarajevo.
Total war transformed economies, governments, and gender roles.
1917: February Revolution then Bolshevik seizure in October.
Versailles punished Germany and fueled resentment.
Depression enabled fascist and Nazi rise.
Appeasement failed; WWII and the Holocaust followed.
commonMistakes: Blaming WWI on a single cause.
Confusing the February and October Revolutions.
Saying the United States joined the League of Nations.
Treating fascism and communism as identical ideologies.
Underestimating the Eastern Front's role in Germany's defeat.
examTips: Use specific evidence: Article 231, Brest-Litovsk, Munich 1938, Stalingrad.
Compare fascist Italy, Nazi Germany, and Stalin's USSR.
Explain causation for the rise of dictatorships with economic and political factors.
Discuss total war's effects on women and the state.

practice.stem: The immediate trigger for World War I was

choices.text: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo

practice.explanation: The June 1914 assassination set off the July Crisis.

practice.stem: Which was a provision of the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?

choices.text: Germany accepted responsibility for the war and was required to pay reparations.
The United States joined the League of Nations.

practice.explanation: Article 231 and reparations were central and resented.

practice.stem: The Bolsheviks gained support in 1917 by promising

choices.text: an alliance with Germany against Britain

practice.explanation: The slogan appealed to war-weary soldiers, peasants, and workers.

practice.stem: The Munich Agreement (1938) is the best-known example of
practice.explanation: Britain and France allowed Hitler to annex the Sudetenland to avoid war.

practice.stem: Which development best illustrates the concept of total war during World War I?

choices.text: Professional armies fought brief battles far from civilians.
Governments directed industrial production, rationed food, used propaganda, and employed women in munitions factories.
Only volunteers served in the military.

practice.explanation: Entire societies and economies were mobilized.

practice.stem: Lenin's New Economic Policy (1921) differed from War Communism in that it

choices.text: allowed peasants to sell surplus grain and permitted small private businesses

practice.explanation: A tactical retreat to revive the economy after civil war.

practice.stem: Which factor most directly increased support for the Nazi Party in the early 1930s?

choices.text: The strength of the Weimar economy
German victory in World War I
Mass unemployment and economic collapse during the Great Depression

practice.explanation: The Depression discredited Weimar and boosted extremist parties.

practice.stem: Stalin's forced collectivization of agriculture resulted in

choices.text: an immediate rise in peasant living standards
widespread famine and millions of deaths, especially in Ukraine

practice.explanation: Grain requisitions and resistance led to catastrophic famine in the early 1930s.

practice.stem: The principle of self-determination at the Paris Peace Conference resulted most directly in

choices.text: the creation of new states in Eastern Europe such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia
the unification of Germany and Austria
the restoration of the Russian monarchy

practice.explanation: It applied mainly to the defeated empires in Europe, not to colonies.

practice.stem: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942–1943) is significant because it

choices.text: marked a turning point on the Eastern Front, after which the Soviets pushed Germany back
led to Italy's entry into the war

practice.explanation: A German army was destroyed, and momentum shifted to the USSR.

practice.stem: Which statement best compares Nazi Germany and the Stalinist Soviet Union in the 1930s?

choices.text: Both used terror, propaganda, and one-party rule, but Nazism was built on racial ideology and preserved private property, while Stalinism pursued class-based state control of the economy.

practice.explanation: Similar methods, different ideologies and economic structures.

practice.stem: Historians who emphasize the alliance system as a cause of World War I would most likely argue that

choices.text: the war was caused only by Serbian nationalism
commitments among the great powers turned a regional Austro-Serbian conflict into a general European war
colonial competition in Africa directly caused the war
Russia sought to avoid war at all costs

practice.explanation: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria, and France and Britain were drawn in.

practice.stem: Why did the League of Nations fail to prevent aggression in the 1930s?

choices.text: It lacked enforcement power, the United States never joined, and major powers were unwilling to impose meaningful sanctions.
It had a large standing army it refused to use.

practice.explanation: Weak responses to Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Ethiopia exposed its limits.

practice.stem: Which intellectual development of the early 20th century most challenged Enlightenment confidence in human rationality?

choices.text: Freud's argument that unconscious drives shape human behavior

practice.explanation: Psychoanalysis suggested irrational forces drive behavior.

parts.prompt: Describe ONE way the Treaty of Versailles contributed to political instability in Germany in the period 1919–1933.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the Great Depression affected European politics in the 1930s.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain ONE reason Britain and France pursued appeasement toward Germany in the 1930s.

rubric.description: E.g., war guilt clause and reparations fueled resentment; the 'stab-in-the-back' myth undermined Weimar; reparations contributed to hyperinflation.
E.g., unemployment boosted extremist parties (Nazis, communists); democracies weakened; governments expanded economic intervention.
E.g., memories of WWI losses and public desire for peace; belief Versailles was too harsh; military unpreparedness; fear of communism; economic constraints.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The treaty's war guilt clause and heavy reparations humiliated many Germans, who blamed the Weimar government for accepting them; nationalists used this resentment to attack the republic's legitimacy.

(b) In Germany, the Depression caused mass unemployment that discredited the Weimar government, and voters turned to the Nazis, who became the largest party in the Reichstag by 1932, leading to Hitler's appointment as chancellor in 1933.

(c) British and French leaders remembered the enormous losses of World War I and faced public opinion strongly opposed to another war, so they made concessions such as allowing the annexation of the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938.
